name: Pedro Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a small carpentry crew making concrete forms and timber braces on a school hall site. I have a vocational trade certificate and I can square a difficult form quickly, but our small contractor pays me below the usual carpenter rate. I like teaching the crew a clean setup; late timber deliveries leave us with unpaid gaps.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner does cleaning shifts, and our two school-age children live with us in a mortgaged home. We have less than a month of expenses saved and only a few similar builders nearby. I use AI every day to check material lists, but I check every length on the drawing and I take wage questions to our builders' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school hall crew that faster forms are welcome, but someone still has to brace the concrete forms and check the pour. I would also say our small contractor should pay its best site hands better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the lead carpenter but paid below the trade norm, and we have less than a month of bills saved. My partner's cleaning shifts vary, so even without a new machine, one missed site week puts the mortgage under strain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the hall formwork and use my daily AI tool for the timber list, checking its lengths against the drawings. At the next builders' union meeting I'll bring our wage slips and ask the representative to raise minimum shift notice and pay with the contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious already, if I'm honest. A neat AI site form doesn't cover a school lunch or a mortgage payment when a carpentry shift is cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on the shortened pour day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a late timber delivery shortened the pour day, and two workers were sent home early. I stayed to reset the braces, but the lost hours still showed on the family's budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the union representative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring three recent payslips and the cancelled-shift message to the union representative. If we can get a written notice rule, workers can plan childcare before the site gate opens.

say: **Formwork checks** and braces remain hands-on despite quicker forms.
Our contractor should improve **shift notice and pay** for experienced workers.
think: My **lead role** still pays below the trade norm.
Less than a month of **savings** leaves the mortgage exposed to cancelled shifts.
do: **Lead** school hall formwork and check AI timber list against drawings.
**Bring** wage slips and cancelled-shift message to builders' union meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings and variable household hours even with mild AI.
S0.quote: A neat AI site form doesn't cover a school lunch or a mortgage payment when a carpentry shift is cancelled.
fieldNote: His **low pay** and thin savings explain anxiety in the plateau, despite high skill and a continuing site role.
He already uses **AI daily** for lists and seeks a concrete union rule about pay and shift notice.

steps.text: Lead school hall formwork and check daily AI timber list
Bring wage slips and cancelled-shift message to builders union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI may order panels and set pour schedules before robots handle the panels themselves. The contractor should not use a faster office calendar to call us in for half a paid day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My formwork skill is still needed, but AI buying could make the firm run fewer people on unpredictable shifts. We cannot float a bad month on the small amount in our account, and there are few similar local sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the next four AI-generated panel orders with what the crew fits and show any errors to the site manager. I'll also ask the union representative to put a minimum paid callout and a human review of shortened shifts on the next workplace agenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about fewer paid hours, even if no robot can brace a wall yet. I know a tidy schedule can hide an empty pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a wrong panel order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the exact panel size on the order before the lorry loads, then show the mismatch to the manager. A missing formwork panel makes the whole site crew wait for wages it may not get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the shift-pay request become group action?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the shift notices and payslips to a group meeting, not just complain over lunch. The union representative can ask management to answer everyone together.

say: **AI buying** changes orders before robots handle site formwork.
A faster office schedule must not mean **half-paid callouts** for crews.
think: My **formwork skill** remains useful, but unpredictable paid hours could shrink.
Our **thin account** and few local sites leave little room for a bad month.
do: **Compare** four AI panel orders with fitted formwork sizes.
**Ask** builders' union to raise minimum paid callouts at workplace meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about shorter paid days under faster office scheduling.
S1.quote: A missing formwork panel makes the whole site crew wait for wages it may not get.
fieldNote: He sees a realistic **paid-hour risk** from scheduling, though physical formwork changes more slowly.
His response joins **measured order checks** to a specific union meeting about minimum paid callouts.

steps.text: Compare four AI panel orders with fitted school hall formwork
Ask builders union to raise minimum paid site callouts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can plan the pour, but capable robots around 2031 could set the forms. We should demand a paid transition before the firm cuts the people who trained its crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 48 when the robots can do hands-on construction work. With less than a month saved, few nearby jobs and two children at school, even losing one regular site week each month would break our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll call the union organiser and ask for a meeting on written crew numbers, paid training time and notice. If our contractor offers a funded robot-site safety course with wages during class, I'll enrol and attend; if it cuts my shifts, I'll apply only to posted local construction jobs that cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect this small contractor to cut a large part of the formwork roster if the robot works, and I have lain awake counting what a missed month would do. I still have a plan to put to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about a lost week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we may have to pause the children's paid activities if a full site week goes. I would not pretend the tiny reserve can carry the mortgage while I sit in an unpaid class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms would count as a transition offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a published roster, a named paid trainer and wages through the course. A site robot video is not a training place, and a promise of future construction work is not a posted job.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans pours before robots set forms around 2031.
The contractor should publish **crew numbers** and paid transition terms before cuts.
think: At about **48**, losing regular formwork shifts could break our mortgage budget.
Our **under-month reserve** and few local jobs leave little room to wait.
do: **Call** union organiser for meeting on crew numbers and paid training.
**Enrol** in funded robot-site safety course if wages continue during class.
**Apply** after shift cuts only to posted local jobs covering mortgage.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major roster cuts and sleepless worry, while still planning.
S2.quote: A site robot video is not a training place, and a promise of future construction work is not a posted job.
fieldNote: He expects a **major roster cut** and reports sleeplessness, making alarmed grounded in his household's thin reserve.
His course needs **funding and class wages**; his fallback needs an actual posted local job paying enough for the mortgage.

steps.text: Call union organiser for crew numbers and paid-training meeting
Enrol in funded robot-site safety course if class wages continue
Apply after shift cuts to posted local construction job covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 thinking AI changes pour plans, while robots around 2034 threaten our hands-on formwork. Five years should be used to bargain for paid site retraining, not spent watching a sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 51 at the robot date and still paying the mortgage. My skills give me a say in how forms are tested, but low pay and less than a month saved mean I cannot leave work for an unpaid qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll bring a draft training agreement to the union workshop next month, asking for fees and paid release for a recognised building-services certificate. If the contractor signs those terms and gives me a place, I'll enrol next intake; until then I'll lead the formwork crew and keep the wage coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the hours, but five years lets me organise instead of waking up to a cut next week. I want the agreement signed before the first robot trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a site robot trial test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the crew to test a form panel on an uneven foundation and record the braces and rework. A factory demonstration on a flat floor tells us little about a live site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly must paid release cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid release means my usual wage for every assessment day, plus the course fee covered. If the offer drops either part, I cannot take it while the mortgage needs this week's pay.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes plans before robots set formwork around 2034.
Workers need a **signed paid-training agreement**, not a sales video.
think: At about **51**, I still need the site wage for the mortgage.
My **thin reserve** rules out unpaid course days despite my site leadership.
do: **Bring** paid training agreement to next union workshop.
**Enrol** in recognised building-services course if signed funding, paid release and place exist.
**Lead** formwork crew while waiting for those written terms.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with more time for bargaining and training.
S3.quote: A factory demonstration on a flat floor tells us little about a live site.
fieldNote: His five-year plan is **collective bargaining** for course fees and usual wages during assessment, followed by actual conditional enrolment.
He retains **paid site work** unless the written funding and real course place materialise; the tiny reserve cannot cover unpaid days.

steps.text: Bring paid course agreement to next builders union workshop
Enrol in recognised building-services course if signed funding, paid release and place exist
Lead formwork crew while awaiting paid course terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 could draw the hall and robots around 2039 might set the forms. Ten years is enough for workers to demand proper pay and build a second skill while there is still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 56 when capable robots arrive, and I cannot assume the mortgage will be gone. Even with time, our low pay and under-month buffer keep the household close to the edge if site hours change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union's training group for a funded, evening building inspection course with a real place next term. If the fees are covered and I can keep all paid shifts, I'll enrol; I'll also keep a monthly record of our mortgage payment and cancelled site hours to bring to wage talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money as much as a robot a decade away, though I have time to get the crew organised. I don't want ten years to become an excuse to keep paying us less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about evening classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show our children why I go to evening classes, if a funded place opens. I would tell them the course is to keep a wage in the house, not because their school costs are their fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the wage record be used?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My record of cancelled site shifts would show exactly which lost hours ate into the mortgage money. I would take it to the union wage meeting rather than asking the children to cut everything first.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes drawings before robots set forms around 2039.
A decade allows **funded training** and wage bargaining while paid work continues.
think: At about **56**, the mortgage may still need my formwork wage.
Our **low pay** and tiny reserve make present cancelled shifts a worry too.
do: **Request** funded evening inspection place through union training group.
**Enrol** next term if fees covered and all paid site shifts continue.
**Bring** mortgage and cancelled-shift record to union wage meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about today's income and future robots, with time to organise.
S4.quote: My record of cancelled site shifts would show exactly which lost hours ate into the mortgage money.
fieldNote: His long-run response combines **paid work** with group bargaining and conditional actual study, matching progressive views and a thin cushion.
Even in a decade scenario, **current cancelled shifts** keep him anxious; the children are not treated as a budget fix.

steps.text: Request funded evening inspection place through union training group
Enrol in evening inspection course if fees covered and site wages continue
Bring mortgage and cancelled-shift record to union wage meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest: robots around 2031 could cut formwork shifts while the mortgage is already close to the edge. A written crew plan, paid training and a union-backed minimum shift payment would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the carpenter when an AI purchase order leaves a panel off the truck. A missing form panel can erase a day's wages before any robot sets foot on the site. Workers should not carry that cost alone.

headlineQuote: A missing form panel can erase a day's wages before any robot sets foot on the site.
portrait: **Pedro**, 43, leads school hall formwork with a vocational trade certificate and strong practical skill.
His **below-trade pay**, partner's variable cleaning shifts and mortgage leave less than a month of expenses saved.
He uses **AI daily**, has few nearby building jobs and asks the builders' union for wage and training terms.
Possible site-hour cuts make him **anxious**; a fast robot rollout alarms him because he expects major cuts and reports sleeplessness.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring formwork robots around 2031 while the mortgage already strains a tiny reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, paid training and a union-backed minimum shift payment would let workers plan without unpaid gaps.
